Recorded experiment · select, transform, compare

From a matching shape
to an action

A symmetry can describe how one part relates to another. Here we also use that relationship as an instruction: select a route, apply a small native action, and compare the generated route with an existing target.

Start with two overlapping T readings, then change the action bits yourself. The source stays available, and every result shows exactly which comparison was checked.

Two readings, shared strokesAction laboratoryThe eighteen-pattern corpusCandidate enginesLimits and counterexamplesFull study
Reusable native substitutions, displacements and traversal correspondences, with bounded recurrence search over the 18 authored atlas readings. This is an executable symmetry study, not autonomous concept discovery, a global minimum-description search, material transfer or geometric settlement.
18Patterns79Engines117Distinct unordered route pairs147Whole-route action witnesses240Actions5Templates2T readings5Controls

Two readings can use the same stroke

The whole route is shown first. Green and rust identify the two selected windows; gold marks their shared section references. The three smaller drawings then separate the selected source, the native action output, and the target already present in the ornament.

A2 · overlapping reads

Two open T-shaped boundaries

Seven-edge windows share three actual source sections. The transformed copy predicts the second window; the original overlapping reads reference one path. These are open T-shaped outlines, not three-way native junctions.

First windowSecond windowShared native sections

The gold sections are referenced by both readings. The highlighted windows do not add another physical stroke to the source.

B6 · overlapping reads

Two decorated T-shaped boundaries

Fifteen-edge windows share seven actual source sections. The curled flanges belong to a decorated T/corridor read. Literal T contacts against the framing rail are a separate projected read; their native course and rail are not welded.

First windowSecond windowShared native sections

The gold sections are referenced by both readings. The highlighted windows do not add another physical stroke to the source.

Try the action bits

Choose a route, change one bit, and inspect the captured result. Three bits select a planar basis action. The fourth changes traversal. Displacement is a separate native word, so moving a copy is not hidden inside its orientation.

These controls select precomputed native Gojo applications. The browser draws their captured points; it does not invent or execute the transformation.

What each bit means

The displayed word is b3 b2 b1 b0. This is the small action grammar used by this experiment; it does not replace the ODV encoding or merge its distinct meanings.

PositionActionExact interpretation
b3Reverse traversalReverse the section order and each section's endpoint order, independently of the basis action.
b2Oppose V imageReverse the ordered target direction selected for input V.
b1Oppose H imageReverse the ordered target direction selected for input H.
b0Exchange axesChoose V as the image of H, and H as the image of V.

Read the same possibilities across eighteen patterns

The search is bounded by its supplied paths, windows and action grammar. Candidate counts are overlapping explanations. They are not independent quality votes, an exhaustive set of engines, or probabilities of historical construction.

Each unordered route pair is counted once. The expandable action-witness table keeps the alternative transformations that match those pairs. The smallest seed is taken from any single route, including small inserts; it does not rank the complexity of the complete pattern.

What a match does—and does not—establish

These controls keep positional agreement, traversal and native site-sharing available as separate questions.

A reflection predicts the directed path

Horizontal steps are unchanged; vertical steps reverse. Source and copy have independent site identities with the same alias pattern.

Ordered geometry matchesSite-sharing pattern: yes

Same turns; different reach

The reflected action misses one changed reach. Similar turn order is weaker than exact correspondence; no settlement silently repairs it.

Ordered geometry does not matchSite-sharing pattern: yes

Same coordinates; broken handoffs

The support matches, but each section has independent endpoints. Coordinate equality does not prove path continuity.

Ordered geometry matchesSite-sharing pattern: no

Same support; reversed traversal

Reflection alone cannot explain the target's order. A support-only read would lose this distinction.

Ordered geometry does not matchSite-sharing pattern: yes

Reflection and reversal together

Adding the separate traversal correspondence accounts for the reversed target without changing the basis law.

Ordered geometry matchesSite-sharing pattern: yes

  • A2 and B6 admit overlapping boundary readings produced by vertical reflection plus advance. Shared source sections are one piece of evidence read twice, not duplicate material.
  • Vertical reflection changes vertical direction in the selected frame; it does not itself reverse horizontal motion. Reversing traversal changes both the order and each directed section.
  • One small instruction can describe a witnessed correspondence and generate a fresh copy on a different input. The application and match still retain separate evidence.
  • The smallest tested seed is conditional on this grammar and on the chosen realization. It is not an original-engine probability or a complete storage-cost estimate.
  • Topology, ordered motion, equal reaches, geometric support and projected crossings are different invariants. A shared silhouette does not imply shared routes or physical junctions.
  • A desired rectangle or hexagon can next be a connected target claim. Turning mismatch into change still needs explicit response routes, movable parameters, resistance and retained unresolved tension; this study does not add an unseen shape solver.

Symmetry as a reusable action

What this experiment is for

A pattern can contain a familiar shape without having been drawn one whole shape at a time. Two neighboring readings may share several of the same sections. A small repeated action can also generate a larger shape that crosses the action's repeat boundaries.

This study brings those relationships into view. It asks what small action can repeat a piece of an existing ornament, what the action preserves, and what it changes. It also examines two different meanings of a T in a meander: an open T-shaped boundary and a literal projected three-arm contact. These are useful reads, but they are not the same native structure.

Start with A2. Its short hook word can be repeated in opposed vertical frames. Then select a larger seven-section boundary. That boundary resembles an open T, and its neighboring copy shares three actual sections with it. The shared sections are read twice; no new material is drawn.

B6 extends this idea with a deeper inward return. Its larger boundary reads overlap over seven sections. Its framing also produces actual T-shaped projected contacts, whose material routing remains a separate question.

The examples use the declared centre-line reconstructions from the source survey. They test those connected realizations. They do not automatically trace the photographs, recover an original drawing history, or establish that one explanation is the uniquely correct engine.

Three things that must remain distinct

A match says that a selected transformation takes one observed part to another part under a stated correspondence. It does not change either part.

An action supplies an input surface, transformation structure, displacement, and output. Repeating that action can produce a new course. An action that matches one pair of pieces may still fail when repeated again.

Settlement would introduce change into a connected local system and let its relations account for that change. A newly drawn or transformed path does not establish that such a response mechanism ran.

The action audit checks repeated generation rather than fitting a new correction at every step: the previous generated output becomes the next input. If an action drifts away from the observed course, that mismatch remains visible. There is no hidden adjustment to the target after each application.

Each application creates new sites while preserving the input's internal shared-site pattern. Equal coordinates at the seam between two generated chunks do not weld those chunks together. The observed course already has its own connected handoffs; a generating machine must explicitly retain or establish the corresponding seam. The present repetition controller is a finite chain of applications, not an independently running or self-modifying loop.

A2: a small engine and a larger overlapping read

The authored A2 course begins with these points in its own common-reach frame:

p0 (0,2) -> p1 (3,2) -> p2 (3,1) -> p3 (2,1) -> p4 (2,0)
         -> p5 (5,0) -> p6 (5,1) -> p7 (4,1) -> p8 (4,2)

It then repeats with a horizontal displacement of four common-reach units. These are coordinates of the declared realization, not recovered physical measurements of the source image. Section e0 joins p0 to p1, section e1 joins p1 to p2, and so on. The section numbering continues through the whole course.

The first four sections and the next four sections correspond under:

F(x,y) = (x + 2, 2 - y)

This is reflection about the local horizontal axis y = 1, followed by a horizontal displacement. The order of traversal is preserved. Applying it twice gives a translation by four; the reflected frame returns to its original orientation after two applications.

The larger T-shaped reads use a different cut through the same course:

Read Actual course sections Ordered points
First open T boundary e1 through e7 (3,2), (3,1), (2,1), (2,0), (5,0), (5,1), (4,1), (4,2)
Next opposed boundary e5 through e11 (5,0), (5,1), (4,1), (4,2), (7,2), (7,1), (6,1), (6,0)
Their common participation e5, e6, e7 The same three source sections in both selections

The same action F maps the first ordered boundary to the second. A seven-edge read therefore advances by four edges and overlaps its neighbor by three. There is no requirement that a useful concept occupy one exclusive block of storage, one whole pen, or one generating step.

This is an open outline with a mouth between its two ends. Naming its silhouette a T does not add a closing segment, fill its interior, or create a three-way junction. A white-region read would also need to retain its boundary, mouth, and selected outside context.

The same outline has additional support symmetries. A suitable half-turn can match it when the traversal correspondence is reversed. That is a different action from the direct vertical reflection used above, even if a renderer without arrows makes their outputs look identical.

B6: the same relation with more internal detail

The B6 inner course begins with a sixteen-section word. Its first eight sections map to the next eight under:

G(x,y) = (x + 4, -4 - y)

This reflects about the local horizontal axis y = -2 and advances by four. Applying it twice translates by eight. The outer framing is another selected participation; it is not silently included in the inner course's word.

Read Actual course sections Relation
First larger boundary e1 through e15 Starts at (7,0) and ends at (8,0)
Next opposed boundary e9 through e23 Starts at (11,-4) and ends at (12,-4)
Their common participation e9 through e15 Seven identical source sections, shared by reference
Ordered correspondence First boundary to next boundary Apply G without reversing traversal

The B6 boundary has inward returns on its arms. At full detail it is not the straight-edged T outline of A2. A coarser description can retain the open mouth and paired arms while exposing the extra return structure as detail. Calling both examples T-like is a candidate abstraction, not proof that their complete section words are equal.

The exact overlapping-read relation is stronger and simpler to verify than a general T classification: the selected source sections are known, the transform is explicit, the image matches in order, and the overlap is actual shared participation. That evidence can remain useful even if we later choose a different verbal name for the shape.

B6 also has literal projected T contacts

At (7,0), the inner course arrives from the left along e0 and turns downward along e1. A framing contribution extends from (7,0) to (8,0). Their projection has left, right, and downward arms, but the frame's coincident endpoint is not the course's native shared endpoint.

At (4,-4), the inner course arrives from above along e7 and turns right along e8. A framing contribution arrives from the left. Its projection has left, right, and upward arms.

Contact Inner course participation Additional framing participation
(7,0) Path 0: e0 then e1; left-to-down turn Path 4: its section 0, (7,0) -> (8,0)
(4,-4) Path 0: e7 then e8; above-to-right turn Path 1: its section 0, (0,-4) -> (4,-4)

Select one common-reach unit of each outward arm. Reflection and translation (x,y) -> (x + 3, -4 - y) take the second contact's projected T support to the first contact's support. However, the ownership and directed handoff do not match under that support-only correspondence: one native course uses the upper and right arms, while the other uses the left and lower arms. The third arm is provided by a different route in each case.

This is an example of a true coarse match with a meaningful finer mismatch. The image can support a common T-shaped contact, while the native route reads still distinguish the possible flow behavior. A switching or merging law would require a further explicit connection. Coordinate coincidence supplies neither that law nor a material weld.

A small code for a selected action grammar

For this experiment, an action can be summarized by four local bits. Displayed as b3 b2 b1 b0, they select:

Bit Meaning in this local grammar
b0 Exchange the two basis axes.
b1 Oppose the image of the source horizontal basis.
b2 Oppose the image of the source vertical basis.
b3 Reverse the ordered traversal correspondence.

Together, the first three bits describe eight signed basis permutations; the last bit distinguishes the two traversal orders. The displacement is additional connected structure. These four bits are a compact read of this grammar, not the complete encoding of a path or a universal replacement for ODV.

The canonical action keeps its native map rows, displacement word, and ordered marker correspondence connected. A reader can derive the compact code from that surface. The code must not become the only place the transformation means anything.

For A2, the compact code is 0100. Its actual substitution rows are H+ -> H+, H- -> H-, V+ -> V-, and V- -> V+. The displacement word is H+ H+ V+ V+, and the ordered marker pair remains in its original order. B6 uses the same four substitution rows with a different displacement word: four H+ reaches and four V- reaches. The different offsets place the reflection axes and the next repeated piece in their respective local frames.

Adding traversal reversal changes this local code to 1100. It also changes the connected marker correspondence; it is not a label that can be changed without changing what the action does.

For an unswapped basis, reversing only the vertical basis changes upward motion to downward motion and leaves horizontal motion unchanged. It does not turn a rightward horizontal move into a leftward one. Reversing the path's traversal does reverse every directed step and reverses the step order. A half-turn opposes both spatial axes while retaining the traversal order unless reversal is separately selected.

Turn handedness alone cannot distinguish all these cases. Reflection exchanges left and right turns; traversal reversal also exchanges them. Combining both can preserve the turn word while changing the directed correspondence. Endpoint, basis, and ownership evidence therefore remain relevant.

What the bounded engine audit can say

The audit searches a declared, finite family. Within each eligible course it considers chunk widths that divide the section count, eight basis permutations, both traversal orders, and a constant displacement fitted from the first correspondence. Each proposed action is then applied repeatedly to its previous generated output and checked against the observed course.

For each action, the report retains its shortest successful seed. Whole-route pair checks require at least two sections. Both the ordered geometry and the pattern of shared endpoint identities must match. The search does not cover every partial window, cyclic starting phase, multi-route group, or change of scale. An empty result therefore means no engine was found in the tested family, not that the pattern has no compact explanation.

A shortest seed found by this procedure means shortest within this grammar and this observed course. It is not a globally shortest program, an exhaustive search over all Gojo structures, or a probability that the original artist used that engine. Whole-route pair comparisons likewise check selected transformed correspondences; they do not infer material joins or hidden histories.

Seed-section counts also are not encoded byte costs. An executable explanation has a frame, a displacement, a controller, correspondence, and retained checking evidence in addition to its seed. The study makes those connections inspectable; it does not claim that the current diagnostic representation is maximally packed.

Several descriptions may fit. For example, a smaller hook with a reflecting action and a larger two-hook word with a translating action can reproduce the same finite support. Their different controllers and exposed parameters matter when we ask what can change next.

The corpus contains related examples from the same source sheets, including repeated views of the same family. A construction that appears often here is common in this selected collection. It is not thereby common in all ornament, human drawing, or other domains. Reuse across independent examples and success on unseen variations would supply stronger evidence.

What the recorded run found

The recorded run covers all 18 authored pattern readings. It retains 79 route/action recurrences, and 147 exact action witnesses over 117 distinct whole-route pairs. More than one action can explain the same pair, so those last two counts answer different questions. The action laboratory also validates 240 applications: five templates, sixteen local action codes, and three displacements.

Some useful examples concern the main course, rather than the smallest detail anywhere in the ornament:

Selected course Seed sections Occurrences, including the seed Repeated action
A2 opposed hooks 4 10 Reflect vertically and advance.
B6 deep interlock 8 6 Reflect vertically and advance.
A5 inward-outward winding 14 4 Translate the complete winding, including its central turnaround.
B5 battlement 2 10 Reflect vertically and advance.
CL5 diagonal zigzag 1 8 Reflect vertically and advance.
CR4, each outer strand 2 3 Reflect vertically and advance.
CR4, each inner strand 5 3 Reflect vertically and advance.

Every subsequent occurrence in these rows was produced from the previous generated one and checked natively. The occurrences include the initial seed: A2 therefore has nine validated applications after its first four-section piece, not ten applications after it.

CR4 gives a particularly useful shared mechanism. All four strands use the same repeating action, (x,y) -> (x + 28, 12 - y), but the inner and outer seed words are different. A separate reflection, (x,y) -> (x, 12 - y), matches each strand to its partner. This preserves the distinction between sharing an action and being copies of the same detailed path. The planar action audit does not by itself validate an over/under schedule.

Simple translation recurrences appear in thirteen of the eighteen readings; vertical reflection with advance appears in nine. Quarter-turn recurrences appear in the small squares of A3 and A6. Those repeated inserts strongly affect the totals: A3 and A6 alone contribute fifty of the seventy-nine retained recurrences. Their reported minimum seed of one section describes a small square component, not their whole ornament. These are counts of witnessed candidates, not seventy-nine independent concepts or a ranking of aesthetic quality.

The missing results are informative about the search boundary. B4 and CL6 are collections of independent one-section pens, and the current search does not take a collection of those pens as its repeating seed. Their zero results do not count against their regularity or compactness. CL2 supplies another case: no repeated action was retained within one finite coil, but the whole-route comparison finds correspondences between the separate coils. A collection-level controller is a natural next search scope for these examples.

The five comparison controls also separate the claims as intended. Changing a reach breaks the exact geometric match while retaining the shared-site pattern. Breaking the handoffs preserves the ordered coordinates while failing the shared-site check. A reversed target fails the reflection-only comparison and matches once traversal reversal is explicitly included.

Reusable patterns and informative exceptions

The current collection suggests several compact engine families worth retaining as candidates:

  • Advance with alternating frame: A2 and the B6 inner course use an opposed vertical read on successive chunks, then return to the original frame.
  • One word, several placements: A3, A4, and B3 retain translated copies of the same word with a relative phase. B8 adds a vertical displacement and a separate spot stream.
  • Repeat a mixed group: A3 combines paths with divided-square inserts; A6 combines nested squares with four turned hooks. Each component can remain separately readable.
  • Turn inward, then return: A5 retains a central turnaround and continues outward. CL2 instead retains finite inner ends and half-turned cell placement.
  • Several participants define a crossing or a space: B4, CL6, and CR4 make useful structures available only when more than one path is selected.

The less frequent cases are useful because they expose what a simpler engine omits: finite ends, an extra spot stream, a quarter-turn orbit, an insert, a frame contact, or crossing order. Their cost is not automatically a defect. Their utility must be judged against the question the structure is answering.

Deformation and the next settlement step

A path can be transformed, reparameterized, or edited while retaining a correspondence to its source. Keeping the same native endpoint identities can preserve connectedness and closure. It does not automatically preserve the projected arrangement: moving sections can create or remove contacts, crossings, overlaps, and white openings. Smooth animation alone is not a guarantee that these events cannot occur.

Likewise, matching two patterns after a permitted deformation does not show that either pattern physically settled into the other. This pass supplies actions and checks. Autonomous geometric settlement is not claimed.

A concrete next settlement experiment would need to connect:

exposed path or pair
  -> a measured or qualitative gap/contact read
  -> a connected desired relation and its mismatch
  -> a permitted local response route
  -> signed tension or an explicit structural retargeting operation
  -> changed local state
  -> a new read, with blocked change and remaining tension visible

The response route must say which extent, phase, or site can move, what it must preserve, and what happens when two demands conflict. If the material may not cross another strand, that admissibility must be enforced locally or a failed claim must remain visible. If a boundary is open, the reader must not invent a closing segment simply to improve the score.

A desired rectangle would therefore need connected claims about its ordered sides, opposite relationships, corners, and closure. The word "rectangle" would not select a hidden fitting routine. Adding a corner, removing a section, splitting a branch, or joining two sites would be an explicit structural change, with a new correspondence; it would not be disguised as an adjustment of the old path's values. The original read can remain available alongside the changed candidate when both have utility.

This would turn an observed relationship into an active local mechanism. The deeper opportunity is that the same connected word and transform can serve as a recognizer, a predictor, and a generator, while its selected response laws determine whether it can also adapt.

Gojo ornament studies. Recognition, native action, observed correspondence and future settlement remain separate stages.
